analysis.one_liner: Requires financial regulators to prove a rule's benefits outweigh its costs before it can take effect, and lets companies sue to overturn rules.
analysis.headline: The bill, which would have required financial regulators to prove rules' costs were outweighed by benefits before finalizing them, was introduced by Senator Shelby and six Republican cosponsors in March 2013 and never received a vote, dying in the Senate Banking Committee.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill, introduced by Senator Richard Shelby, would have forced every major financial regulator — including the SEC, CFTC, FDIC, and the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau — to run detailed cost-benefit analyses before proposing or finalizing any rule, and barred agencies from finalizing a rule whose quantified costs exceeded its quantified benefits. It would have let companies sue in federal court to overturn rules on procedural grounds, required agencies to periodically review and streamline existing rules, and created a Council of agency chief economists reporting to Congress. It was referred to the Senate Banking Committee and never received a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Banks, securities firms, and other financial companies regulated by the SEC, CFTC, FDIC, Federal Reserve, and CFPB. The bill would have made it much harder and slower for those agencies to issue new rules, and given regulated firms a new route to sue and get rules thrown out if an agency's cost analysis fell short. Financial trade associations have historically sought exactly this kind of analysis requirement, arguing post-crisis rules were too costly.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Banks and financial firms facing regulation

how_it_helps.text: It gives banks, securities firms, and other regulated companies extensive new procedural grounds to challenge rules in court: a person adversely affected by a regulation could sue in the D.C. Circuit, and a judge must vacate the rule if the agency's analysis falls short.

It blocks agencies from finalizing any rule where quantified costs exceed quantified benefits, and it exempts Federal Reserve monetary policy decisions from the requirements while sweeping in the CFPB, SEC, FDIC, and other market regulators.
It requires agencies to publish plans to modify or repeal existing regulations every five years and to report their cumulative burden on the economy.

analysis.who_pays: Ordinary people who rely on the securities markets, banks, and consumer financial protections. Cost-benefit analysis is hard when benefits — a prevented fraud, a systemic risk averted, a predatory loan not made — are difficult to quantify in dollars, while compliance costs are easy to count; a strict 'costs must not exceed quantified benefits' bar plus court challenges would have made many consumer and market-stability rules legally fragile or impossible.
analysis.who_pays_short: Consumers and investors relying on financial safeguards

drawbacks.text: The bill bans an agency from finalizing any rule whose quantified costs exceed quantified benefits — a bar many genuine safeguards cannot clear, because benefits like avoided fraud or a prevented financial crisis are hard to put a dollar figure on while compliance costs are easy to count.

It creates a one-year window for regulated companies to sue in federal appeals court, and a judge must strike down a rule if the agency's paperwork falls short of the required analysis — giving regulated firms a routine tool to delay or kill rules regardless of the rule's merits.

By mandating multi-year analysis cycles and five-year retrospective reviews, the bill would have slowed the implementation of the 2010 Dodd-Frank financial reforms, leaving gaps in oversight of banks and derivatives markets.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The transparency and lookback-review ideas have some merit — agencies should show their work and occasionally check whether rules worked. But the core mechanism, a hard cost-benefit veto plus litigation that vacates rules on procedural grounds, is heavily weighted against regulation: many real financial harms (fraud, hidden risk, predatory lending) are hard to quantify, so the hardest rules to defend would die even when their benefits are real. The bill never got that far to test this: it died in committee without a hearing-recorded vote, so the design tradeoffs were never resolved.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the Senate Banking Committee the day it was introduced and sat there without action until the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Introduced March 5, 2013, the bill was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs.
No further action was taken for the rest of the 113th Congress: no committee vote, no Senate floor debate, and no House counterpart action recorded in the bill's history.
The bill expired when the 113th Congress ended on January 3, 2015.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The banks and financial firms that would have faced new rules under Dodd-Frank implementation — the bill's death left the regulators' authority intact — while no one else was directly better or worse off because nothing changed.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Financial firms that would have faced new rules

sides.party_line_note: All seven sponsors and cosponsors were Republicans; no Democrats signed on, and the Democratic-controlled Senate committee never took the bill up.

industries.industry: Banks, securities firms, and other regulated financial companies
industries.note: The bill would have added heavy procedural hurdles — cost-benefit vetoes, reproducible data requirements, and a litigation window — to every rule from the SEC, CFTC, Fed, FDIC, and CFPB, and let courts vacate rules on analysis grounds. Regulated firms gain delay and leverage.

industries.industry: Federal financial regulators (CFPB, SEC, CFTC, FDIC, FHFA, OCC, NCUA)
industries.note: The bill would have subjected these agencies to a uniform analysis regime, constrained their rulemaking authority, and created a Council of their own economists reporting to Congress — a structural check on their independence.

In principle, better analysis could catch bad rules, and small businesses get an explicit assessment of whether they bear disproportionate burdens. In practice, the cost-benefit bar and litigation access would mainly slow the consumer protections these agencies write.
